catalog_quote: 1.3 Stress. In the following examples, stress is marked by an acute accent (´) over the vowel of the stressed syllable. 1) Stress usually occurs on the next to last syllable of words: báso, migbása, medáet, mengábat, menenóo, meáma. 2) For words in which the next to last vowel is e and the last vowel is other than e, stress occurs on the last syllable: begás, lekát, etebáy, benál, binelesán. 3) For words in which the last two vowels are both e, stress occurs on the next to last syllable: déleg, bénget, isélem, minéles. 4) A few words, contrary to the above rules, occur with stress on the last syllable: edén, sinú, ontô, ekéd, ikâ, olô, pedén. ... [sec. 1.2:] The mid central vowel e is always pronounced as a very short vowel sound. It has the sound of the vowel in the English word but (ebel, kebkeb, mebenes, doen). ... Locator (p. 6, sec. 1.3; 1.2 p. 3; 1.4 p. 6; 1.5 p. 7) is correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1976 SIL grammar sketch (169 pp per Glottolog) by the principal field linguist of the language; it is the only grammar/sketch in Glottolog's 20-item bibliography, there is no phonology monograph, dissertation, JIPA illustration or instrumental study, and the statement is explicit, rule-formatted and exemplified, with the schwa ('very short' mid central e) as the sole weight criterion — so the 'weight / full-vs-reduced-vowel / right edge / default penult' coding follows directly from the text.
